title: Sydney police investigate second possible mistaken identity shooting in two days
description: Police in Sydney are investigating a second possible mistaken identity killing at the hands of organised crime in less than 48 hours.About 15:15 local
body: Police in Sydney are investigating a second possible mistaken identity killing at the hands of organised crime in less than 48 hours.About 15:15 local time on Wednesday, emergency services rushed to a home in Merrylands West after reports a man in his 40s had been targeted in a drive-by shooting. He died at the scene.A day earlier, about 03:40 on Tuesday, a university student in his 20s with no criminal ties, was shot during a home invasion in Glen Alpine in the city's southwest. He also died at the scene.Police say the Tuesday shooting appears to be an "innocent life" taken by organised crime while Wednesday's fatal attack may have targeted the "wrong person".Police believe the man had arrived at the Merrylands West home just moments before he was shot in the doorway.Asked if investigators were treating the case as a suspected mistaken identity, police said: "Tragically, that is a possibility that the wrong person has been shot by these offenders"."The victim has no links that we are aware of to organised crime, however he has associated with people that reside at this address," Det Supt Simon Glasser said on Wednesday.The residents of the home were "very well known to police" with links to organised crime, but the man who was shot was "quite likely" a business associate, Glasser said.Earlier, New South Wales Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon had described Tuesday's  killing of Marco Tapia, a university student who was only known to police over a traffic offence, as "completely unacceptable"."The fact that what appears to be an innocent life was taken [on Tuesday] is something that no community should accept and no community should live in fear of violence,"  Lanyon said."I don't want any innocent member of the community to be impacted by organised crime. We will not tolerate it."Shortly after Tuesday's fatal shooting, a known organised crime figure posted in a message on social media: "popped the wrong person, didn't even get the right house". Earlier this year, a Sydney grandfather was allegedly kidnapped and murdered in what police believe was a case of mistaken identity.Chris Baghsarian, 85, was taken from his home in a pre-dawn raid and his body was found two weeks later near a golf course. Several people have been arrested and charged in the matter.And last year a Sydney plumber was shot dead in front of his family home in what police said was also a case of mistaken identity.

schema.headline: Sydney police investigate second possible mistaken identity shooting in two days

title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
description: Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immedia
body: Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immediate cap on donations.Florence Eshalomi said a new team would be "working at pace to find a solution", as some MPs expressed concerns over the influence of wealthy individuals donating large sums of money.The Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, but ministers have been pressed to go further by introducing a limit for UK-based donors.Reform UK's Danny Kruger warned the Representation of the People Bill was a "flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap" the party.Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors.There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving £1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers. Last year he gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.One of her proposals called for an immediate £500,000 limit which would reduce to £100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap. The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed."But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics"."That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.  "I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested £50,000 a year.Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at £100,000 annually.Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than £100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.

schema.headline: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says

title: DNB: Netherlands bank moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move
description: The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "incre
body: The Dutch central bank (DNB) has confirmed that billions of dollars in gold has been taken out of north America and relocated to London, citing "increasing geopolitical unrest".DNB said on Wednesday that 86 tonnes of gold had been removed from the US and Canada in a complex operation that took several months. It is now being held by the Bank of England, where the precious metal can be traded more easily "in a crisis situation".Bank president Olaf Sleijpen said the move was "necessary to strengthen our resilience and preparedness".The decision comes amid an ongoing trade dispute between the US and Canada, with both countries announcing fresh tariffs on each other after failed trade talks.DNB said the transfer, which took place between March and August, saw 27 tonnes of gold bars moved from New York and Ottawa to Zeist in the Netherlands. A similar quantity and quality was then moved to London, with no need to melt the bars down.Exactly how so much gold was transported across the Atlantic Ocean has not been revealed.The rest of the transfer was carried out by selling the gold in New York, and repurchasing it in London, the bank said, external."Combining the processes of buying and selling and physical transport has allowed DNB to spread the risks associated with such a complex physical gold relocation," the statement said.DNB did not confirm what it was referring to with its mention of "geopolitical unrest" but the US economy remains in an uncertain position due to the country's ongoing war with Iran, which has impacted global trade.Canada, meanwhile, has been hit hard by US tariffs on its key sectors of steel, aluminium, lumber and automobiles as well as an additional 50% levy on about C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) of Canadian goods announced in August. DNB said that gold that is held with the Bank of England "is regarded as the world's most easily tradable gold," and therefore more readily available in a crisis than if it was still in the US or Canada.Prior to Wednesday's announcement, the DNB held 31.3% of its gold in New York and 19.7% in Ottawa. This has now fallen to 18.5% in both countries.The total Dutch gold stock was 612.4 tonnes at the end of 2025 and has been valued at €72.2 billion, DNB said.The bank's share of gold in London has increased from 18.1% to 32.1% after the move, while it still holds 30.8% of its reserves in the Netherlands.

schema.headline: DNB: Netherlands bank moves billions in gold to London in 'crisis preparedness' move

title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
description: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in
body: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core. Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces."I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else."I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently?

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference

title: The Gentlemen: Stars of Netflix show react to Meghan speculation at series 2 premiere
description: ‘I'd be the last to know’: Stars of The Gentlemen react to Meghan reportsFigure caption, Stars of The Gentlemen react to Meghan rumoursByNoor NanjiCul
body: ‘I'd be the last to know’: Stars of The Gentlemen react to Meghan reportsFigure caption, Stars of The Gentlemen react to Meghan rumoursByNoor NanjiCulture correspondent at GuildhallIt has been almost two weeks since reports emerged that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks for a role in The Gentlemen.At the world premiere for series two of the Netflix show on Wednesday night, stars including Maya Jama, Hugh Bonneville and Theo James remained tight-lipped about the prospect of Meghan joining the cast.“It’s fascinating to watch, but ultimately it’s a lot of rumour,” James told BBC News, while Jama said: “I’d be the last person to know!”The show’s executive producer said he didn't want to say yes or no to the reports about Meghan, but added they were looking forward to “more energy and surprises” to come.The Gentlemen, a comedy action series about a duke turned drug baron, created by Guy Ritchie, was a major hit when it first dropped in 2024.The show has officially been greenlit for a third series. Talks with Meghan are understood to be in the early stages, but the details of the discussions and any role she might be offered have not yet been revealed.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ray Winstone, Theo James, Kaya Scodelario and Guy Ritchie pose for pictures at the premiere of The Gentlemen series 2The drizzle cleared up as stars arrived at Guildhall, with Vinnie Jones, Kaya Scodelario, Joely Richardson and Ray Winstone all in attendance.When asked about the reports regarding Meghan, Jones said he's heard “only what you have".But he joked: “We’ve got a lot of pretty women in this. So I’m not sure there’s room for any more.”"Way above my pay grade," Scodelario said, while Bonneville commented he had “no idea” if there was any truth to the rumours."Prince Harry's in it," declared James. "He's playing one of my love interests."Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understandsJama, meanwhile, said that as a newcomer herself to the cast, she had no tips to share with Meghan.“Oh my God, she’s a seasoned actor. I have no advice for her. She knows what she’s doing,” added Jama.Ritchie, who also attended the premiere, did not speak to the press. But writer and executive producer Matthew Read told BBC News they were looking forward to "bringing up more energy and surprises in series two and further on in the series”.Not a no then, I asked."I just don't think it's right to speculate at this stage, so I wouldn't like to say yes or no,” he added.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Theo James and Kaya Scodelario play lead roles Eddie Halstead and Susie GlassIn the first series, Eddie Halstead (played by James) inherited his wealthy family's country estate following his father's death, much to the fury of his older brother Freddy. He then discovers the estate is partly being used to grow cannabis for an extremely successful underground drug empire.This time around, the criminal enterprise is expanding out of the British countryside and into the lush lakeside setting of Italy.On the second series, James said: "If you're going to do it, you've got to make sure it's better."So we worked, I hope, pretty hard to make sure we evolve the world. It was more complex, and we had more character development."'We've raised the stakes'That was echoed by Scodelario, who plays one of the show's toughest and most assured characters, Susie Glass. She runs the cannabis farm under the estate's grounds."We've really tried to raise the stakes as much as possible," she said. "Some of the episodes take a much darker turn, but we still have the fun and the joy that everyone really liked about it."Bonneville, another newcomer to the cast for series two, said working with Ritchie was "wonderfully chaotic, but with a great purpose in mind".The actor, who previously starred in Downton Abbey, also joked there was no difference between the period drama and the criminal underworld of The Gentlemen. "It was exactly the same world," he said."No, it was fun to enter this slightly skewed world of the perverted aristocracy up to no good," he added."I'm sure it was going on at Downton Abbey, but now the lid is lifted on what really happens in these stately homes."The Gentlemen series two is released on Netflix on 3 September.

schema.headline: The Gentlemen: Stars of Netflix show react to Meghan speculation at series 2 premiere

title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
description: Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of
body: Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.He blamed the previous Tory government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, meaning Wednesday was the first time he had faced Badenoch at PMQs.Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998. This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain its spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK,  announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill."The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said."He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts."Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality."I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government.Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict."Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said."Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years."How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages."She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."In the Tory reshuffle, Andrew Griffith replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor.Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."

schema.headline: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge

title: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death
description: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn -
body: Two men and two women have appeared in court charged with murdering a baby girl who had been repeatedly stabbed at a house in Sheffield.The newborn - referred to as Baby S in court - was found at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area, on Sunday, having suffered 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings.Andrea Skopova, 20, formerly of Robey Street, Sheffield, and Peter Horvath, 19, Nina Horvathova, 37, and Peter Horvath, 38, all of Holywell Heights, appeared at Sheffield Magistrates' Court.The four Slovakian nationals have been charged with murder, causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant.A fifth person, a 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, also appeared in the same court charged with perverting the course of justice.All five defendants were remanded into custody to appear at Sheffield Crown Court on Thursday. Tuesday's hearing was told the baby's body was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse and was wrapped in a towel inside a blue bag.Prosecutor Luke Hopkinson said the defendants had been accused of perverting the course of justice by cleaning the scene.Earlier, police said two women, aged 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remained on bail.Speaking ahead of the court hearing, Det Ch Insp Tom Woodward said: "This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl."I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation."We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course."Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl."Police said officers would continue to be in and around the Holywell Heights area carrying out inquiries. Listen to highlights from South Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, catch up with the latest episode of Look North

schema.headline: Four people in court charged over Wincobank newborn baby death

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
description: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig
body: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned that Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack last month on Leipzig airport."We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better," von der Leyen said. Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the whole alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".Russia has rejected German accusations that a drone carrying explosives deliberately targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August.The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil"."We will not tolerate it," she said.While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said they were working on how to tighten enforcement of existing sanctions, and added there was broad support for an EU visa entry ban on Russian ex-combatants as well as stricter visa limits on Russian tourists.Several EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, are pushing for more than €193bn (£165bn) in frozen Russian assets to be used to help Ukraine. The idea was first planned at the end of 2025, and rejected by Belgium where the money is held. However, Belgium's position is unchanged because it fears being held financially liable by the courts.The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole."We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.High-voltage power lines were damaged near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at Skarżysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent men, women and children in Ukraine".

schema.headline: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig

title: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two sailors, Saudi Arabia says
description: Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.The Saudi
body: Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.The Saudi national shipping company, Bahri, confirmed on Wednesday that its vessel Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz".Sidr was hit by projectiles north of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, according to maritime security firms. A South Korean-owned supertanker, Senegal Prosperity, was reportedly struck east of Musandam around the same time.Iran has not responded to the Saudi allegation. But it said earlier that two tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while using an unauthorised route through the strait.The news of the sailors' deaths came after the US military carried out a wave of air strikes on Iran and Iranian forces targeted US bases in neighbouring Arab states with missiles and drones in their biggest exchange of fire since July.On Wednesday Iran's health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 injured in the US attacks. Iran has accused the US of a "war crime" over a strike that killed four people including two children at a wedding party in the southern city of Sirik. The US military said it was looking into the reports.Shipping company Bahri's statement said the unspecified "security incident" affecting Sidr happened in the Strait of Hormuz at around 23:40 local time (19:40 GMT) on Monday."It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident," it added. "The company extends its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathies to their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time."Later, the Saudi foreign ministry expressed the kingdom's condemnation of "Iran's targeting of the Saudi tanker (Sidr) while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz".It also condemned the recent Iranian attacks on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, and stressed the "need to halt escalation and respect the security and safety of international navigation", as well as the security of global energy supplies, national sovereignty, and international law.The statements were issued a day after maritime risk management and intelligence firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers each loaded with two million barrels of Saudi crude oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other as they transited outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday.Sidr was struck by "unknown projectiles" at 19:52 GMT about 16 nautical miles (30km) north-east of Khasab, Oman, while Senegal Prosperity was struck by "three unknown projectiles" about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, according to Marisks.The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency also reported two incidents in the same locations.On Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said in a statement that two oil tankers sought "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz before "striking mines and exploding". The vessels were "currently on fire", it added.The US military has not commented, but it said the latest strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members".The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports.The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.Despite the Iranian attacks, US President Donald Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday - a record daily total since the start of the war.

title: Is sleep tracking making your sleep worse?
description: Chasing a perfect sleep score? You could be making it worse ByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of
body: Chasing a perfect sleep score? You could be making it worse ByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield.Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep.While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation with sleep is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn.So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep?'Sleep scores are completely made up'The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score".But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London."There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers."Figure caption, How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worseHare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients."I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds."It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it."One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims"."We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Daytime impactStudies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate.In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept.The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times.Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake.'Cycle of worrying'This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago."I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC."I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things."Image source, Jess HillImage caption, Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three yearsHer "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept."I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says.The BBC has approached Garmin for comment.Image caption, Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually feltDr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping."The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures."He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says."If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep."So how can we actually sleep well?Hare recommends:Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish."Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock.Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability".Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it".

title: Will Lindsay Clancy trial end in a mistrial? Here are the options
description: Figure caption, Watch: What happens now after Lindsay Clancy trial jurors deadlocked again?ByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdated 2 h
body: Figure caption, Watch: What happens now after Lindsay Clancy trial jurors deadlocked again?ByAna Faguyreporting from court in MassachusettsUpdated 2 hours agoAfter a gruelling five-week murder trial, Lindsay Clancy's fate rests with 12 anonymous jurors. And they cannot make up their minds.The jury of nine women and three men have told the judge, two days in a row, that they cannot reach a unanimous decision. Despite the judge's continued urging that jurors keep at it, the struggle has raised the prospect of a mistrial in Clancy's case."It is desired that the case be decided," Judge William Sullivan told the panel on Wednesday afternoon, after members sent him a second note saying they are undecided after five days. He read a mandatory, formal set of instructions and sent them back - some with frustrated expressions on their faces.The 36-year-old former nurse does not dispute that she killed her two sons and daughter in 2023 in the basement of their family home in Massachusetts. But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and therefore could not distinguish right from wrong.The prosecution claimed Clancy made a calculated, intentional decision to kill them and knew right from wrong in that moment. She is charged with three counts of first-degree murder.Under US law, the jury must unanimously reach a conclusion "beyond a reasonable doubt". If they cannot, the judge can call a mistrial, which ends the trial with no verdict.This jury has several outcomes to choose from. Potential verdicts include not guilty, not guilty by reason of insanity, first-degree murder, second-degree murder, and manslaughter.Mistrial Jurors in Clancy's trial have signalled they are deadlocked and having a hard time coming to a unanimous decision, which is mandatory for any verdict.In the state of Massachusetts, there are typically multiple steps before they can give up. A judge usually tries to pressure the panel to continue deliberating until there's no possible chance of a decision. We've hit two of those steps so far. On Wednesday, Sullivan issued additional instructions, known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge in the state. It's a last-ditch effort, encouraging the panel to consider all perspectives, and ensuring jurors are questioning and examining their own views in the case. It also instructs them to strive to come to an agreement - while maintaining their own convictions and keeping to their individual judgement and conscience. If the jury continues to signal they cannot come to a consensus, it's possible the judge could then declare a mistrial, ending the trial with no decision. A hung jury does not mean prosecutors have proven their case, nor does it mean the defendant is not guilty. The prosecution can then either refile and restart with a new jury, or negotiate a plea agreement. Alternatively, prosecutors can dismiss the charges altogether.Either way, though, Clancy would not go immediately free. She would remain held under the same murder charges in the mental health facility where she is housed now, as her lawyers and prosecutors mull next steps in the case. Image source, ReutersNot guilty / not guilty by reason of insanityThis hinges on the postpartum psychosis defence - her legal team argued that Clancy hallucinated a voice that told her to kill the children.Expert witnesses told the court how severe this illness can be, and family members testified about Clancy's state of mind.Under Massachusetts law, there is no burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness and that she lacked criminal responsibility.Rather, it is on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that she was criminally responsible when she killed her children, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.They can do this by either proving beyond reasonable doubt that she didn't suffer from a mental illness at the time or that, while she had a mental illness, she still controlled her actions and knew they were wrong.A not guilty verdict would mean Clancy went free but that is considered highly unlikely. Much more likely is a not guilty by reason of insanity, which would result in Clancy being detained at a hospital."The case really comes down to where she is going to serve the rest of her life; the defence thinks it should be a psychiatric facility, the prosecution thinks it should be in a state prison," Hershon said.Figure caption, Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?First-degree murderThis is the most serious potential outcome for Clancy - being found guilty of first-degree murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.In the state of Massachusetts, this conviction carries a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.Clancy would effectively need to be seen as "a monster in the jury's eyes" if jurors picked this outcome, Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC.Jurors would have to find there was extreme atrocity or cruelty, or premeditation or both to convict Clancy of this, and it would mean the prosecution had proven there were no mitigating factors.In this case, mental disease or defect - as the law describes it - could be a mitigating factor.Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said during closing arguments there was no dispute Clancy was suffering from mental illness but it was not so severe that she didn't know right from wrong.Expert witnesses for the prosecution cast doubt on whether Clancy actually heard the voice that she said ordered her to kill her children.Second-degree murderThis is a catch-all for any murder that is not first-degree, under Massachusetts law.It applies to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning."For this verdict, the jurors may not be convinced that the actions leading up to the murder rose to the level of pre-planned [or] premeditated but that instead, Clancy consciously saw an opportunity to commit the killings at the specified time," Cucolo said.In the case of second-degree murder, Clancy would also face a life sentence - but with the possibility of parole.ManslaughterThe jury received yet another option when the judge allowed it to find Clancy guilty of manslaughter - previously a point of contention between the defence and the prosecution.A manslaughter conviction would mean Clancy unintentionally killed "by wanton and reckless conduct", which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.The manslaughter option says that through an involuntary intoxication, in this case an overprescription of her medication, Clancy experienced a mental defect that was a mitigator in her understanding what she was doing, Hershon said.Intent is an important distinction between a verdict like manslaughter and the two murder verdicts, experts said."This option allows the jury to accept that the murders were not planned or calculated but that instead Clancy made a split-second decision to act," Cucolo said.The prosecution is not obligated to demonstrate that she intended to cause the children's deaths for there to be a manslaughter conviction, she added.

schema.headline: Will Lindsay Clancy trial end in a mistrial? Here are the options

title: Tara Davis-Woodhall 'lucky to be alive' after car crash
description: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.The 27-year-old America
body: Olympic long jump champion Tara Davis-Woodhall says she is "lucky and blessed to be alive" after being involved in a car crash.The 27-year-old American was on her way to training last week when she was involved in a "very scary" head-on collision, leaving her with a "severe" concussion. While not ruling herself out of this month's inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championships in Budapest, the reigning world champion says she has been unable to train since the accident."Luckily I walked away without any major injuries," Davis-Woodhall wrote on social media."At this point I'm working with my team and doctors to get healthy, but I'm not sure if I will be ready to compete at Ultimate Championships next week. More updates to come."Davis-Woodhall said her injuries were not life-threatening but that both cars, which were going at about 20mph, were written off.  "It's really unfortunate timing; I am at the peak of my training right now," she said. "I'm as fast as I've ever been. I'm as strong as I've ever been. So this decision is very difficult for me. I don't know where I am right now."The championships in Hungary start on 11 September, where athletes will compete for a top prize of £111,000.The competition brings together Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, as well as the year's leading performers in a three-day end-of-season event. Davis-Woodhall won long jump gold at the 2024 Olympics in Paris, before winning the Worlds in Tokyo a year later.

schema.headline: Tara Davis-Woodhall 'lucky to be alive' after car crash

title: Joshua vs Fury: Tyson Fury calls Anthony Joshua a 'coward' as wait continues
description: Tyson Fury has labelled Anthony Joshua a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight bout can be
body: Tyson Fury has labelled Anthony Joshua a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight bout can be agreed.The long-time rivals had been expected to finally settle their differences and face off in November, but the likelihood of that happening is diminishing as an agreement over the venue has yet to be reached.Two-time unified world champion Joshua and his Matchroom promoter Eddie Hearn have signed a contract for the fight to take place in the United Kingdom, while the fight's organisers are understood to favour staging it in the United States.Hearn has previously said the contracts would have to be renegotiated if the fight were to take place outside the United Kingdom.On Wednesday, Fury, who defeated journeyman Mariusz Wach last month to keep the potential blockbuster clash with Joshua on track, said negotiations over the fight were becoming "quite tiring"."I've been down to fight at every location that's been mentioned - England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York," said the 38-year-old."Listen, I've said yep, yep, yep, yep, yep, every single time. Zero stipulations."The facts are I feel like you're being a coward. I feel like you don't want the fight and you're just conning everybody. I feel like you've been doing that for years."You've had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you've never really wanted it, so let's see if you're going to man up for a final time."In a separate post, Fury continued to taunt Joshua, 36, this time alongside former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson, telling his fellow Brit to "sign the contract, big boy" as he paid homage to Tyson's iconic line.Queensbury's Frank Warren, who promotes Fury, told Sky Sports News his fighter was "100%" signed up for the fight."It is signed by Tyson," said Warren. "Tyson is signed up for the fight and agreed for the fight."

schema.headline: Joshua vs Fury: Tyson Fury calls Anthony Joshua a 'coward' as wait continues

title: US Open 2026 results: Katie Boulter wins just one game in 58-minute US Open defeat by Karolina Muchova
description: British number one Katie Boulter endured a "bad day at the office" as she won just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Wimbledon runner-up Karolina
body: British number one Katie Boulter endured a "bad day at the office" as she won just one game in a 58-minute demolition by Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova in the US Open second round.The match, originally scheduled to be played on one of the outer courts, was moved to the 14,000-capacity Louis Armstrong Stadium after heavy rain in New York.But fans who had counted themselves lucky to have gained a third match on their day session ticket may have been left feeling short-changed, as Boulter fell to a swift 6-1 6-0 defeat by the Czech seventh seed."Ultimately, it was a bad day at the office – times two," said Boulter."I struggled with the conditions. I struggled with the roof, the noise, I let things distract me."I let it get to me. I'm not usually aware of everything going on. It made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. I have to deal with it better."Fellow Britons Jacob Fearnley and Toby Samuel failed to reach the men's third round on Wednesday, both losing to seeded players in Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry and Jiri Lehecka of the Czech Republic.But Francesca Jones had better fortune as she returned to win her first-round match against Poland's Magda Linette after it was interrupted by rain on Tuesday.Boulter's serve let her down as she hit eight double faults and no aces, while she won just 33% of points behind her first serve.Unable to fend off any of the seven break points she faced, the 30-year-old was not helped by an unforced error count of 22 compared to just four winners.In comparison, two-time US Open semi-finalist Muchova landed 14 winners and just nine unforced errors as she impressed with smart drop shots and piercing groundstrokes."I would be really humbled [if I was Boulter], I would sit down with my team and say 'OK, we need to change something big time'," former world number five Daniela Hantuchova told BBC Radio 5 Live."First of all, it was very obvious today that it was the serve. I feel like it needs to be cleared up because she was losing the rhythm and not using her legs. That's the number one thing."If I am Boulter, I would be on the practice court tomorrow. If she still wants to invest everything into her tennis then she needs to be on the court."Boulter has had plenty to celebrate in her personal life this summer after marrying Australia's Alex de Minaur, the world number seven, in July.However, it has been a disappointing tennis season for the world number 62, with just two wins across the four Grand Slam tournaments.Since suffering a first-round exit at Wimbledon, Boulter has won just two of the six matches she has played.Jones had won the first set 6-4 against Linette, ranked 82nd, when the rain put a halt to proceedings on Tuesday night.When the pair returned on Wednesday, it was Linette who appeared fresher as she raced to a 5-0 lead and wrapped up the second set in 28 minutes."I've never been quite in this position so I was nervous with how I'd quite feel about coming back out," Jones told Sky Sports afterwards."I thought I'd maybe handle it better than the score reflects."Jones rallied back in the decider, claiming the decisive break at 2-1 before completing the victory - just her second at Grand Slam level.She will play American 14th seed Iva Jovic in the second round on Thursday."[I'm] really grateful that I just managed to pull through," said Jones."She came out all guns blazing - it was incredible how she was playing until about 4-0 and then it started to equal out. But in that situation, hats off if they can sustain that, I just tried to show my northern grit, stick in there and do what I can."Fearnley had produced a remarkable five-set comeback against Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round, but the British lucky loser's fortune ran out in a 6-3 6-3 3-6 6-3 defeat by against Etcheverry.The Argentine 27th seed recovered from losing the third set and falling a break behind in the fourth, while Fearnley's 57 unforced errors and 11 double faults ultimately proved costly.Samuel, 23, won through qualifying to reach round two on his US Open debut, but was beaten 6-4 6-2 6-4 by 18th seed Lehecka.Meanwhile, British number three Jan Choinski fell to a 6-3 6-1 7-6 (7-5) defeat by Dutchman Botic van de Zandschulp in a first-round match that had also been pushed back to Wednesday because of the rain.
